doc.title: Bobby Militello interviewed by Monk Rowe, Buffalo, New York, October 14, 2002

title: Theory lessons with Joey Azzorello; listening to Cannonball and pianists
summary: Piano lessons gave a theory basis; he explains rootless voicings, 'no wrong note', and how pianists can put a soloist in a box.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: And Joey started giving me theory lessons and the Mehegan Book and started to say well this is what you found out. This is sort of what that is and this is what the substitute changes represent from your theory. And so we started going through that thing. I’d never really followed that through real far, I think I studied with him for about six months. But the idea was that my head opened up to a new process and that was that I never had to just blatantly play what was in front of my face. Because that truly is jazz. You are always trying to interpret it. So after that point, as you picked up on a little while ago, I’m very much an ear player. And so what it was now, the process was, listen to other things. Listen to Trane. Listen to Cannonball, which I listened to a lot to Cannonball. I mean I think I sound like Cannonball, or I try to. That’s the sound in my mind’s ear that I try and achieve is that roundness and that beautiful shaped, centered tone. I mean I try and do that. And through hearing them blowing on tunes and listening and listening and listening more and more, and then later Hubert Laws and listening to how he transcended anything having to do with just the normal change that was being played, and then listening to piano players, who all comped, the better players, McCoy and those cats and Bill Evans and the different people behind cats, and Bill Evans behind Miles and Trane and all that kind of stuff. When you listen to Red Garland when he first was starting you are hearing the fact that no longer did they give you the root. They skipped the root out. They pulled that root out and they went third and seven in the left hand sometimes, and then just the upper extension in the right hand. So in the key of C, if you’re playing a C7 they might

play a B triad in the right hand and just, you know, E and B flat down here. And what happens is when you do this there is the D change to play on, there’s the C7 to play on, but because there’s no root, you’ve got multiple changes to play on from the left hand and you’ve got multiple changes to play on because you’ve got a new key here, you’ve got the left hand key which is not giving you the key of C so you’ve got a whole bunch you can play on there. All of a sudden I’m listening to this and saying — revelation. Wait a minute. There is really no wrong note. Technically there is no wrong note, you can play anything. It’s where you’re going, or where you came from. So now get the ear to understand that. Get the ear, but the limitations are when you play with a piano player who doesn’t play with the freedom to give you those voicings that my ears say the notes that I’m going to play that normally would be right with a piano player who knows what he’s doing, or no piano player at all, right? Now my ear says, no no, you can’t do that now because he’s stopping you, which is a pet peeve of a lot of soloists. And that’s the piano player can put you in a box.
